Pre-Islamic poetry was, simply by being poetry, one form of social awareness. As such, it also represented a particular stage in the development of that awareness through artistic expression. But poetry tells us more than this. Its texts also contain signs of other forms of awareness among the pre-Islamic Arabs. The clearest example is religious awareness, which at its core expresses a way of understanding the relationship between human beings and the world.

Pre-Islamic poetry contains many signs of this kind. We can use them to trace the forms religious awareness took, the directions in which it was developing, and the level it had reached in the period immediately before Islam.
Take, for example, this line by a pre-Islamic poet:
Yaghūth led us against Murād, and before dawn we had overcome them.

Yaghūth was one of the well-known idols worshipped by the Arabs. The verse therefore tells us something about what its worshippers believed: they imagined that such idols had supernatural powers and could give them victory over their enemies in war.
Or take these lines by the poet al-Mutalammis:
Until she drank her fill there, as night drew near, after the stillness, when the church bells stirred her.

Here we can see the presence of Christianity in the pre-Islamic Arab world. Pre-Islamic poetry contains many such references, and they are widely reported both by early historians and by modern historians of Arabic literature, especially poetry. The same is true of Judaism. Pre-Islamic poetry also gives us evidence of its presence in Arab society before Islam.

If we look historically at the religious ideas found in pre-Islamic poetry—both polytheistic and monotheistic—we are led to an important conclusion. This poetry reflects a gradual movement in religious thought toward belief in one God.

That movement was itself an indirect expression of a broader change taking place in society. During the sixth century CE, at least in the northern part of the Arabian Peninsula, social life was beginning to move beyond a world made up of many separate tribal units. These tribes existed largely on their own and were constantly fighting one another for reasons rooted in older clan relations.

The direction of change was now beginning to weaken this fragmented tribal order. New economic and social forces were entering the old system and putting pressure on the narrow relationships of the closed tribe.

Trade and money exchange were expanding rapidly across the peninsula. More and more of this activity was being drawn toward one main center: the Quraysh leadership in Mecca, represented by the leading figures of the Dār al-Nadwa, the House of Assembly.

This economic and social movement toward greater unity had to find some form of expression in the awareness of the people living through it. And that is what happened. It appeared in poetry, with poetry’s own particular character, and it also appeared more broadly in religion.
In poetry, we can see it clearly in the work of the outlaw poets, whose poetry expressed a rebellion against tribal relations.

In religion, it began to appear in the movement of the ḥanīfs, who rejected idol worship and called for belief in one God. Their appearance marked the beginning of a revolt against polytheism, which was the religious expression of a society divided into many separate tribal groups.

Pre-Islamic poetry itself became one of the first means through which the monotheistic message of the ḥanīfs was expressed and spread. That message was an early sign that a new Arab social reality, a new social awareness, and a new Arab consciousness were beginning to emerge. In other words, it was one of the developments preparing the way for the rise of Islam.

Pre-Islamic poetry carried the message of the ḥanīfs in verses attributed to some of the leading figures in this monotheistic movement, including Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Suwayd ibn ʿĀmir al-Muṣṭaliqī, and others.
In one passage attributed to Umayya, he says of the ḥanīf faith:
Every religion, on the Day of Judgment before God, except the faith of the ḥanīfs, is false.
And Zayd ibn Nufayl is said to have written:
One Lord, or a thousand lords— which shall I worship when things are divided?
I have cast aside al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā together. That is what the firm and patient man does.

Here we have a clear expression of monotheism through the rejection of religious plurality. This is the position that most clearly defines the meaning of the ḥanīf movement because it fits the historical reality most closely.

The rise of the ḥanīfs reflected a change already taking place in society. Social relations were moving toward a new form in which tribal division was no longer the main organizing principle. Social differences within society were becoming increasingly important instead.

This change in the material foundations of pre-Islamic society helped create the conditions for social awareness to develop toward the idea of one God. The later rise of Islam gave that idea its full historical expression on the social, intellectual, and ideological levels.
Proverbs can also reveal a great deal because they form another historical marker of pre-Islamic Arab culture.

At that stage, Arab culture was still mainly an oral culture. It grew directly out of everyday life and was passed on through speech rather than writing. In a culture of this kind, proverbs are among the simplest and most effective ways of expressing ideas and spreading them widely.
Under these historical conditions, a proverb combines two related qualities.

On the one hand, it can condense a particular event or situation into a short expression. On the other, it can turn that expression into a symbol, lifting the original event out of its individual setting and giving it a broader, more general meaning.
Because proverbs do both things, they can preserve historical evidence about many details of social life and about the different forms of social awareness.

The proverbs of the pre-Islamic Arabs in the period leading into Islam naturally contain this kind of evidence. They show how people viewed ordinary objects, everyday events, and practical situations. They also show how they thought about broader human questions and problems, within the historical limits of their time.

In these proverbs, we find the life of pre-Islamic Arabs and their reflections on relations between people in the different areas of human activity familiar to them. We find their moral standards, emotional states, alliances, loyalties, conflicts, and many different kinds of experience drawn from their actual conditions of life.
What concerns us most here, however, is the kind of knowledge these proverbs preserve about nature, society, and thought. This is what allows us to treat them, in some sense, as a cultural marker.

Pre-Islamic proverbs contain a great deal of such evidence, provided that we always read it within its historical setting. In other words, we must judge its value as knowledge according to the level of development reached by Arabian society at the time.
On this basis, we can learn something about their knowledge of the universe, society, and nature from sayings such as:
“Beware the green growth on the dung heap.”
“The barren land has grown rich with pasture.”
“Like the ostrich: neither bird nor camel.”
“It is my house that is stingy, not I.”
“Killing is the strongest deterrent to killing.”
“The one who abandons you is the killer’s brother.”
“Not everything white is fat, and not everything black is a date.”

Alongside proverbs of this relatively limited cultural kind, we should also consider another type that shows a higher level of cultural development. These are proverbs that express their meaning through artistic metaphor and therefore show a greater degree of aesthetic development.

There is also the saying that a flood drove a man to thirst, used for someone who falls into hardship because of abundance, or who receives harm from something that should have brought good.
There is, however, a problem here similar to the problem we encountered with pre-Islamic poetry: how sure can we be that these proverbs really date from the pre-Islamic period?

Arab proverbs from before and after Islam became mixed together, and many sayings were attributed to the pre-Islamic period only later, during the age when oral material was being written down. The same motives that are said to have led people in the Islamic period to compose poetry and attribute it to pre-Islamic poets may also have led them to invent proverbs and assign them to the same period.

Still, there are clues that can make the pre-Islamic origin of some sayings more likely, including some of the examples just quoted. Some clues come from the language of the proverb. Others come from its style. Others are connected to the historical event said to have produced it.
There is no need to examine this question in detail here.
We should also remember that Arabs in the pre-Islamic period did not live only inside the Arabian Peninsula.
They had communities and centers of activity in neighboring regions, where they came into contact with other peoples and ways of life. These included Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine, and eastern Egypt.
Levels of social and economic development therefore varied across the Arab world, and levels of intellectual development naturally varied with them.

Differences could even be seen among the main centers within the Arabian Peninsula itself: Mecca, Medina—then known as Yathrib—and Ṭāʾif in the north, and Ṣanʿāʾ and the other towns and fertile centers of Yemen in the south.
It may even be fair to say that Mecca stood apart during this period. Its economic and social development showed features more advanced than those found in much of the rest of the peninsula.

One reason was that Mecca had drawn much of the higher tribal leadership into its orbit. This allowed its leading families to control the care of the Kaʿba, where the religious symbols of different tribes were gathered in the form of idols and other objects of worship. Many of these belonged to the strongest tribes and to those most closely connected with the commercial traffic moving along the great caravan routes between the north and south of the peninsula.

The leaders of Mecca used their religious responsibility for the Kaʿba and for pilgrimage during the sacred months as a means of holding commercial markets in Mecca. It also helped them dominate internal and external trade and strengthen the position of the Meccan aristocracy. They did this in the name of protecting the rituals associated with the Kaʿba and providing the many services required by visiting pilgrims.
Those services even included literature, which was the highest form of cultural expression in pre-Islamic society.
In practical terms, the religious pilgrimage seasons were also trading seasons. At the same time, they became occasions for the public recitation of poetry.

This was especially true of the market of ʿUkāẓ, where poets and orators took part in something close to a public contest. A poet whose poem won the approval and admiration of the assembled delegations could become the star of the season. If he had previously been unknown, his reputation might suddenly spread across the peninsula and then pass into history.
This literary tradition encouraged poets to spend more time refining their poems and bringing them to a level worthy of public competition and pride.

It also helped create and develop traditions and rules of literary criticism. In other words, it produced another, more advanced form of aesthetic and intellectual awareness within pre-Islamic society.

Poetry recitals were already accompanied by acts of criticism. According to established custom, someone among the assembled delegations would be recognized as having the ability to judge the artistic quality of poetry. The audience would listen to his judgment after the recitation. That judgment could then become the basis of the poet’s fame, the spread of his work, and what we might call critical debate about the poetry of the season—and even about the judge’s decision itself.
Like poetry, public speaking in pre-Islamic Arabia was at once an intellectual, artistic, and religious phenomenon. It also carries much the same historical evidence as pre-Islamic poetry.

Like the poet, the orator served as a spokesman for his people—that is, for his tribe. He defended them, praised them, challenged their enemies, and upheld the tribe’s values, positions, and established relationships.

But in the final period before Islam, some orators began to move in a direction similar to that of the soothsayers. They used speeches as a form of preaching and as a way of encouraging reflection on questions about the universe, society, and morality.

Their speeches therefore often relied on short phrases designed to make an immediate impact. The language was tightly rhetorical, with balanced and rhyming endings. It was compressed and forceful, using every resource available to the speaker to strike the listener’s ear and mind at once.

Perhaps the best-known example is the famous speech attributed to Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī. Tradition says that the Prophet heard Quss deliver it at the market of ʿUkāẓ, before the rise of Islam, while standing on the back of a “red camel.”
“People, gather together. Listen, and understand. Whoever lives will die. Whoever dies will pass away. And everything that is coming will come.”

“Clear signs: rain and vegetation; fathers and mothers; those who depart and those who come. Stars that move, seas that do not disappear, a roof raised high and a bed spread below. A dark night and a sky filled with constellations.
“Why do I see people die and never return? Are they satisfied and therefore remain where they are? Or are they being held there, asleep?”

Poetry preserved their achievements, increased their standing, struck fear into their enemies, glorified their horsemen, magnified the numbers of their fighting men, and answered the attacks of poets from other tribes.
